0.title: Reading the Last Things
0.overview:
Eschatology — the doctrine of the last things — is among the most contested territories in Christian theology. Christians who agree on virtually everything else have disagreed, sometimes bitterly, about the millennium, the tribulation, the rapture, the nature of the resurrection, and the sequence of events surrounding Christ's return. Those disagreements are real, and this study will not pretend otherwise. But they take place within a framework of convictions that all orthodox Christians share, and it is worth stating that framework clearly before entering the contested territory.

Every orthodox Christian believes that Jesus Christ rose bodily from the dead, that He ascended in that body to the right hand of the Father, and that He will return bodily, visibly, and gloriously at the end of history to judge the living and the dead. Every orthodox Christian believes that history is moving toward a goal — a consummation, a final vindication of God's righteousness, a resurrection of the dead, a new creation — and that this goal is not in doubt because it rests on the word and purpose of the God who raised Jesus from the dead. Every orthodox Christian believes that the return of Christ will be sudden, unexpected, and transformative — "in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye" (1 Cor 15:52).

What Christians disagree about is the sequence and shape of the events surrounding that return: whether there is a literal thousand-year reign before or after it, whether the church will be raptured before a period of great tribulation, whether Israel has a distinct eschatological future separate from the church, and how to read the highly symbolic language of Revelation. This study presents the four main models — Amillennialism, Historic Premillennialism, Dispensational Premillennialism, and Postmillennialism — fairly and clearly, with a final unit offering a Reformed assessment of the strengths and weaknesses of each.
0.theology:
Hermeneutics Is Everything

The single most important factor determining which eschatological model a person holds is not which texts they read but how they read them. All four positions have access to the same Bible; they differ in their interpretive approach to prophetic and apocalyptic literature. The central hermeneutical question is: Should Old Testament prophecy and apocalyptic imagery be read literally or typologically/symbolically? Dispensationalism insists on a consistently literal reading; Reformed covenant theology reads Old Testament prophecy through the lens of New Testament fulfilment, understanding that the New Testament often applies Old Testament imagery in ways that transcend a wooden literalism.

Already and Not Yet

All four positions must grapple with the New Testament's pervasive "already/not yet" tension. The kingdom of God has already come ("the kingdom of God is at hand" — Mark 1:15; "the kingdom of God has come upon you" — Matt 12:28). But it has not yet fully come ("your kingdom come" — Matt 6:10; "maranatha" — 1 Cor 16:22). The resurrection has already begun in Christ ("the firstfruits" — 1 Cor 15:20, 23). But the general resurrection has not yet occurred. Satan has already been bound in a decisive sense (Matt 12:29; John 12:31; Rev 20:2–3). But he still prowls around like a roaring lion (1 Pet 5:8). How each model handles this tension largely determines its structure.

Key Texts in Dispute

The central disputed passage is Revelation 20:1–10, which describes a binding of Satan and a "thousand years" (millennium) during which those who had been beheaded for Christ "came to life and reigned with Christ." Does this describe a future earthly reign of Christ (premillennialism), the present reign of Christ and the church between His first and second comings (amillennialism), or a coming golden age of gospel advance before the return (postmillennialism)? Much also turns on Matthew 24, Daniel 9, 1 Thessalonians 4:13–17, and the interpretation of Old Testament promises to Israel.
0.examples:
Then: The early church held a variety of eschatological views. Justin Martyr and Irenaeus were premillennialists; Origen spiritualised eschatology so thoroughly that he departed from orthodoxy; Augustine, in his mature thought (especially The City of God), articulated what we now call amillennialism and set the trajectory for the dominant Reformed and medieval Catholic reading. The Reformers largely followed Augustine. The rise of dispensationalism in the nineteenth century — through John Nelson Darby and the Plymouth Brethren, popularised by the Scofield Reference Bible (1909) and later by Hal Lindsey's The Late Great Planet Earth and the Left Behind series — represents a dramatic departure from the historic Reformed and church-catholic consensus.

Now: Eschatology matters pastorally, not just academically. How we understand the end shapes how we live in the present: our attitude toward the world (is it redeemable or merely waiting to be destroyed?), our engagement in culture and society (should Christians seek the transformation of institutions or merely rescue souls from a sinking ship?), our understanding of Israel and the Middle East, our posture toward suffering and persecution (is tribulation to be avoided or expected and endured?), and our confidence in the gospel (will it ultimately triumph or be overwhelmed?). These are not idle speculations; they shape mission, politics, pastoral practice, and the spiritual formation of millions of Christians.

1.title: Amillennialism
1.overview:
Amillennialism — despite its name, which means "no millennium" — does not deny a millennium. It interprets the "thousand years" of Revelation 20:1–6 symbolically rather than literally, understanding it as a reference to the entire present age between the first and second comings of Christ, during which Satan is bound (in a qualified sense), the gospel advances through all nations, and the souls of the martyrs reign with Christ (in the intermediate state or in the church's present victorious witness). The millennium is not a future event; it is the age in which we now live.

This is the dominant position of the historic Reformed tradition — held by Augustine, Calvin, the Westminster Divines, the Heidelberg Catechism tradition, Louis Berkhof, Anthony Hoekema, and the majority of Reformed theologians today. It is not a pessimistic position: it does not hold that the church will be overwhelmed before Christ's return. It is a realistic position: the church will face both gospel advance and increasing opposition, both fruit and tribulation, right up to the end — when Christ will return suddenly, the dead will be raised, the living transformed, the final judgment conducted, and the new heaven and new earth inaugurated.

The amillennial reading of Scripture is grounded in a covenant-theological, New Testament-interpretive approach: the New Testament is the lens through which Old Testament prophecy is to be read, and the New Testament consistently applies the promises made to Israel to the church as the new covenant community. The "land" becomes the new creation; the "temple" becomes the body of Christ and the new Jerusalem; the "nation" becomes the people from every nation. There is no separate future programme for ethnic Israel; Israel's promises are fulfilled in Christ and in all who are in Him.
1.theology:
The Binding of Satan

The amillennial reading of Revelation 20:1–3 understands the binding of Satan as a reference to the decisive victory of Christ at the cross and resurrection. Jesus said: "Now is the judgment of this world; now will the ruler of this world be cast out" (John 12:31). In Matthew 12:29, the binding of the strong man is the presupposition of plundering his goods — which is exactly what the gospel mission is doing in this age. The binding is real (Satan cannot prevent the gospel from reaching all nations) but not total (he still operates as "the god of this age" — 2 Cor 4:4, and "a roaring lion" — 1 Pet 5:8). This is the "already/not yet" tension characteristic of all New Testament eschatology.

The First Resurrection

Revelation 20:4–6 describes those who "came to life and reigned with Christ for a thousand years" — the "first resurrection." Amillennialism understands this as a reference either to the regeneration of believers ("passed from death to life" — John 5:24) or to the souls of the martyrs reigning with Christ in the intermediate state. The "second resurrection" (though that term is not used) is the bodily resurrection of all the dead at Christ's return. The first resurrection is spiritual; the second is physical.

One General Resurrection and Judgment

Amillennialism holds to one general resurrection of both the righteous and the wicked at Christ's return (John 5:28–29; Acts 24:15), followed by one final judgment. There is no separate rapture, no seven-year tribulation gap, no earthly millennium after the resurrection. The end sequence is: Christ returns, the dead are raised, the living are transformed, the final judgment is held, and the eternal state begins — new heavens and new earth for the redeemed, and eternal separation from God for the unrepentant.
1.examples:
Then: Augustine's articulation of amillennialism in The City of God (Books 20–22) set the terms of the debate for over a thousand years. He read the millennium of Revelation 20 as the present age of the church — the period between Christ's binding of Satan at the cross and His return. This reading was adopted by the Reformers: Calvin, in his commentaries, reads Revelation in a broadly amillennial framework, and the Westminster Standards assume it. The Belgic Confession and Heidelberg Catechism do not address the millennium explicitly, but their eschatological framework is consistently amillennial. Geerhardus Vos's Biblical Theology and Anthony Hoekema's The Bible and the Future are the most careful modern defences.

Now: Amillennialism is often dismissed as pessimistic or world-denying — an eschatology for those who have given up on cultural engagement. This is a caricature. Hoekema and others have argued that amillennialism, properly understood, provides a more robust foundation for cultural engagement than dispensationalism: if the new creation will be a renewed and transformed cosmos rather than a replacement, then culture-making matters. The present creation is not merely a disposable backdrop for soul-saving; it is the raw material of the new heavens and new earth. This is a profoundly world-affirming eschatology.

verseByVerse.quote: And he seized the dragon, that ancient serpent, who is the devil and Satan, and bound him for a thousand years, and threw him into the pit, and shut it and sealed it over him, so that he might not deceive the nations any longer, until the thousand years were ended. — Revelation 20:2–3
verseByVerse.commentary:
The amillennial reading connects this binding to the decisive victory of the cross and resurrection. Jesus's own words at the time of His death are key: "Now is the judgment of this world; now will the ruler of this world be cast out" (John 12:31). And in Matthew 12:28–29, Jesus declares that His exorcisms demonstrate that the strong man (Satan) has been bound — which is why His goods (captive souls) can be plundered by the advancing kingdom. The binding is not total elimination of Satan's activity but the specific restriction of his ability to "deceive the nations" — i.e., to prevent the gospel from reaching all peoples. This is exactly what the gospel age is: the era in which the nations, formerly held in the darkness of paganism (Acts 14:16; 17:30), are being reached with the gospel.

The premillennialist objects: if Satan is currently bound, why does 1 Peter 5:8 describe him as "a roaring lion"? The amillennial answer: the binding is specific in purpose — he cannot prevent the gospel from reaching all nations — not total in all respects. A chained lion is still a lion; it can still roar and cause harm within the radius its chain permits. The metaphors are not contradictory; they address different aspects of Satan's present activity.

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed and holy is the one who shares in the first resurrection! Over such the second death has no power, but they will be priests of God and of Christ, and they will reign with him for a thousand years. — Revelation 20:6
verseByVerse.commentary:
The "first resurrection" is the critical interpretive question. Premillennialism takes it as a literal, bodily resurrection of believers before the millennium. Amillennialism, following the New Testament's own use of resurrection language, understands it as the regeneration or spiritual resurrection of believers — "passed from death to life" (John 5:24; Eph 2:5–6). Believers are already raised with Christ (Col 3:1) and seated with Him in the heavenly places (Eph 2:6); this present reality of co-reigning with Christ is the "first resurrection."

The pastoral weight of verse 6 is striking: "over such the second death has no power." The second death is the lake of fire (Rev 20:14) — eternal separation from God. Those who share in the first resurrection (regeneration) are exempt from the second death (condemnation). This is not primarily a statement about a future chronological sequence; it is a present comfort for persecuted believers: you have already crossed the decisive threshold — from death to life — and the final death cannot touch you. G. K. Beale's massive commentary on Revelation argues this at length: the first resurrection is the "already" of salvation; the bodily resurrection at Christ's return is the "not yet" of its completion.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not marvel at this, for an hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear his voice and come out, those who have done good to the resurrection of life, and those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment. — John 5:28–29
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus here describes a single "hour" in which all the dead — both righteous and wicked — come out of their tombs. There is no mention of two resurrections separated by a thousand years; there is one event, one "hour," one coming out — differentiated only by its outcome (life or judgment). The amillennialist takes this as decisive evidence against a premillennial sequence of resurrections: Jesus places the resurrection of the righteous and the resurrection of the wicked in the same event, at the same "hour."

The premillennialist responds that "hour" can refer to an extended period, and that Revelation 20 provides additional detail that John 5 does not include. The amillennial reply: when Jesus elsewhere uses "the hour is coming" (John 4:23; 5:25), the "hour" is a specific, unified event — and the parallel structure of verse 29 ("those who have done good" / "those who have done evil" both coming out at the same "hour") makes a sequential reading forced. Acts 24:15 confirms the pattern: "there will be a resurrection of both the just and the unjust" — one event, both categories, one hope.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I saw a new heaven and a new earth, for the first heaven and the first earth had passed away, and the sea was no more. — Revelation 21:1
verseByVerse.commentary:
The amillennial vision of the eternal state is emphatically not the "escape from earth to heaven" of popular Christianity. It is the renewal and transformation of the present creation — a new heavens and new earth in which righteousness dwells (2 Pet 3:13). The word "new" (Greek kainos) means new in quality, not new in the sense of entirely different. The new creation is the present creation redeemed, renewed, and glorified — not replaced. Romans 8:19–22 describes the creation itself groaning in hope of its own liberation from the bondage to decay: the creation is not discarded but liberated.

The "sea was no more" is symbolic in Revelation's framework: the sea represents chaos, separation, and the source of the beast (Rev 13:1). Its disappearance signals the end of all that opposes God and separates humanity from Him. The city that descends — the new Jerusalem (Rev 21:2) — is not a literal cube floating in space but the glorified covenant community, the bride of Christ, dwelling with God in the renewed creation. Anthony Hoekema argued that this vision is the most world-affirming eschatology imaginable: God does not give up on His creation but redeems it, which grounds Christian engagement with culture, art, science, and society in the present age.

2.title: Historic Premillennialism
2.overview:
Historic premillennialism holds that Christ will return to earth before (pre-) a literal thousand-year reign on earth. The return will be preceded by a period of intensifying tribulation and apostasy; the dead in Christ will be raised at His coming; Satan will be bound; and Christ will reign on the renewed earth with His resurrected saints for a thousand years before the final resurrection of the wicked, the last judgment, and the eternal state. The sequence is: tribulation → Christ's return → millennium → final judgment → new creation.

This is called "historic" premillennialism to distinguish it from the newer dispensational variety. It has deep roots in the early church — Justin Martyr, Irenaeus, Tertullian, and Papias all held it — and it does not depend on the dispensational distinction between Israel and the church or on the concept of a secret pre-tribulation rapture. The church goes through the tribulation; Israel has no separate programme from the church; the millennium is an earthly reign of Christ following His visible return. Representatives include George Eldon Ladd, Wayne Grudem, and Graeme Goldsworthy (in his earlier work).

Historic premillennialism reads the New Testament's "already/not yet" tension as pointing to a final phase — the millennium — in which the "not yet" is substantially realised on earth before the final consummation. The present age sees the gospel advancing but also resistance, suffering, and the work of evil. The millennium provides a period of visible, vindicated, earthly kingdom before the eternal state — a demonstration that God's purposes for creation are fulfilled within history, not only beyond it.
2.theology:
The Bodily Return and Resurrection

Historic premillennialism shares with all orthodox eschatology the conviction that Christ's return will be visible, bodily, and glorious (Acts 1:11; Rev 1:7). The distinctive is that this return precedes the millennium and includes the resurrection of believers — the "first resurrection" of Revelation 20:5–6, understood as a literal, bodily resurrection at Christ's coming. This resurrection is distinct from the resurrection of the wicked, which occurs at the end of the millennium (Rev 20:12–13).

Two Resurrections

Historic premillennialism holds to two stages of resurrection: the righteous at Christ's return (1 Thess 4:16: "the dead in Christ will rise first"), and the wicked at the end of the millennium (Rev 20:12–13). The thousand years separates the two resurrections. This reading takes Revelation 20:4–5 as describing a literal, sequential resurrection — "the rest of the dead did not come to life until the thousand years were ended" (v.5).

Differences from Dispensationalism

Historic premillennialism differs from dispensational premillennialism in several key respects: (1) No pre-tribulation rapture — the church endures the tribulation. (2) No separate programme for ethnic Israel — Israel's promises are fulfilled in Christ and the church. (3) No temple rebuilt and sacrifices restored during the millennium. (4) No rigid distinction between the "church age" and the "kingdom age." Historic premillennialism is more compatible with covenant theology and with the Reformed tradition's rejection of a separate future for national Israel.
2.examples:
Then: The early church's premillennialism was rooted in its experience of persecution: the expectation of a glorious earthly vindication of the martyrs — a literal reign of Christ on earth following His return — was a comfort to those who suffered for their faith. Irenaeus (Against Heresies, Book 5) argued for a literal millennium as the completion of God's purposes for the material creation: the earth would be renewed and the saints would reign on it. The premillennialism of the early church was not the dispensationalist system of the nineteenth century; it was a simpler, more doxological expectation of Christ's visible, bodily, earthly triumph.

Now: Historic premillennialism retains significant appeal within Reformed and evangelical circles because it takes the bodily, visible return of Christ seriously as the pivotal event of eschatology, it reads Revelation 20 more literally than amillennialism without the elaborate system of dispensationalism, and it provides a category for the vindication of the martyrs and the completion of God's purposes for the earth before the final eternal state. George Eldon Ladd's The Presence of the Future and A Theology of the New Testament are the most influential modern treatments.

verseByVerse.ref: The Dead in Christ Will Rise First
verseByVerse.quote: For the Lord himself will descend from heaven with a cry of command, with the voice of an archangel, and with the sound of the trumpet of God. And the dead in Christ will rise first. — 1 Thessalonians 4:16
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul's description of the resurrection at Christ's return is vivid, bodily, and public: the Lord descends from heaven with a shout, an archangel's voice, and the trumpet of God — an event no one will miss. "The dead in Christ will rise first" — the resurrection of believers at the parousia is the explicit content of Paul's comfort to the Thessalonians who feared for their Christian dead. The premillennialist reads "first" as indicating that this resurrection precedes something else (the resurrection of the wicked, separated by the millennium) rather than merely that it precedes the catching up of the living (v.17).

The amillennialist reads "first" differently: it means the dead in Christ rise before the living saints are caught up — a sequence within the single event of Christ's return, not a gap of a thousand years. The exegetical question is real, but the pastoral content of the passage is clear in all readings: the dead in Christ are not lost; they will be raised; and those who remain will join them. Paul's purpose is comfort (v.18), not chronological speculation — though the comfort rests on the certainty of the bodily resurrection.

verseByVerse.quote: The rest of the dead did not come to life until the thousand years were ended. This is the first resurrection. — Revelation 20:5
verseByVerse.commentary:
This verse is the pivot of the premillennial-amillennial debate. The premillennialist takes it at face value: the righteous are raised at Christ's return (the first resurrection, vv.4–5), the wicked are raised a thousand years later (after "the thousand years were ended"). The sequence is real and temporal — two resurrections, a thousand years apart. The amillennialist reads the "first resurrection" as spiritual (regeneration) and understands "the rest of the dead" as those who were not spiritually alive in the present age — who will face physical death and judgment together with the righteous at the end.

George Eldon Ladd argued that the natural reading of Revelation 20:4–6 requires a real, bodily resurrection in verse 4 — "they came to life" (Greek ezēsan) — and that the same word in verse 5 must refer to the same kind of event. If the first "came to life" is bodily, the implied second "came to life" (of the rest of the dead) must also be bodily — but separated by a thousand years. This is the strongest exegetical argument for premillennialism, and it carries weight even for those who ultimately prefer the amillennial reading.

verseByVerse.quote: For he must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet. The last enemy to be destroyed is death. — 1 Corinthians 15:25–26
verseByVerse.commentary:
The premillennialist finds in this verse a period of Christ's reign that precedes the final defeat of death — a period during which enemies are progressively subjected to Him. This is the millennium: Christ reigning, enemies being defeated, the last enemy (death) destroyed at the final resurrection that ends the millennium. The sequence supports a premillennial reading: reign first (millennium), then the destruction of the last enemy (general resurrection at the end of the millennium).

The amillennialist reads the "must reign until" differently: Christ is currently reigning ("at the right hand of God" — Rom 8:34; Eph 1:20–22), and He will reign until all enemies are subjected — which is the present age, culminating in the final return. The destruction of death (v.26) is not the end of a millennium but the event of Christ's return and the general resurrection. The passage then continues (v.28): "the Son himself will also be subjected to him who put all things in subjection under him" — suggesting that the end of the reign in view is the consummation of all things in the eternal state, not a transition to a millennium. Both readings are exegetically possible; the passage is genuinely contested.

verseByVerse.quote: I saw the souls of those who had been beheaded for the testimony of Jesus and for the word of God... They came to life and reigned with Christ for a thousand years. — Revelation 20:4
verseByVerse.commentary:
One of the most powerful pastoral arguments for premillennialism is the vindication of the martyrs. Those who were beheaded — killed by the beast's regime — come to life and reign with Christ. The juxtaposition is deliberate: those who lost their heads at the hands of Rome's executioners will one day wear crowns in Christ's kingdom. The humiliation of the martyr is reversed; the throne that condemned them is overthrown; they are raised to reign with the very One for whose testimony they died.

This is eschatology as pastoral comfort and as cosmic justice. The martyrs did not suffer in vain; their suffering will not be the last word; the God who called them to lay down their lives will raise them and vindicate them publicly and visibly. Whether this is understood as the resurrection of the body at Christ's return (premillennialism) or as the present heavenly reign of the martyrs' souls (amillennialism), the pastoral content is identical: the martyrs' witness is eternally honoured, their enemies are judged, and Christ is glorified. Richard Bauckham's work on Revelation shows that this vindication theme — not chronological sequence — is the primary pastoral concern of Revelation 20.

3.title: Dispensational Premillennialism
3.overview:
Dispensational premillennialism is the most widely held eschatological system in evangelical Christianity today, and it has produced some of the most passionate missionary movements, the most earnest expectation of Christ's return, and some of the most serious engagement with biblical prophecy in the modern church. Christians who hold it — including John MacArthur, Chuck Swindoll, J. Vernon McGee, and millions of earnest Bible-believers — do so not because they have been deceived or are reading carelessly, but because they are taking Scripture seriously and following what seems to them the most natural and consistent reading of its prophetic texts.

The system holds that Christ will return before a literal thousand-year reign on earth, and that His return will be preceded by a secret rapture of the church and a seven-year period of tribulation during which God works dramatically among the nation of Israel. It rests on two foundational commitments that deserve to be heard on their own terms: first, a commitment to reading prophetic Scripture with the same literalness we would apply to any other kind of Scripture — if God promised Abraham a literal land, a literal nation, and literal descendants, those promises should be fulfilled literally; second, a recognition that Israel and the church, while both loved by God, appear in Scripture to have distinct identities, distinct roles, and distinct futures, and that conflating them does violence to the specificity of Old Testament promise.

The great strength of dispensationalism is its high regard for the integrity of biblical prophecy. It refuses to let Old Testament promises to Israel simply evaporate into vague spiritual fulfilment. It insists that God means what He says — that when He promised David an eternal throne in Jerusalem, He meant a throne in Jerusalem; that when He promised Israel a restored land and temple, He meant a land and a temple. This is not wooden literalism but a serious commitment to the faithfulness of God to His Word.
3.theology:
The Literal Hermeneutic

The dispensational commitment to consistent literal interpretation is not arbitrary — it flows from a deep conviction about the character of God. If God's promises to Abraham about land, seed, and blessing were fulfilled literally (Abraham did receive a son; his descendants did possess Canaan), then why should His later promises to Israel about restoration, kingdom, and temple be spiritualised away? The dispensationalist argues that the covenant-theological approach of finding all Old Testament promises fulfilled in the church applies a double standard: historical promises are read literally, but future prophetic promises are read spiritually. Consistency, they argue, requires reading all prophecy with the same straightforward literalism.

Israel and the Church

The distinction between Israel and the church is, for the dispensationalist, not a theological imposition but a biblical observation. Paul seems to maintain the distinction carefully: in Romans 9–11 he describes Israel's hardening as temporary — "until the fullness of the Gentiles has come in" (11:25) — and speaks of a future for "all Israel" (11:26) in terms that seem to go beyond merely the elect remnant. He warns Gentile Christians not to be arrogant toward Israel, because God has not rejected His people (11:1–2). The olive tree metaphor (11:17–24) suggests that Israel and the Gentiles are distinct branches — Israel cut off temporarily, Gentiles grafted in, but Israel capable of being grafted back in. This, the dispensationalist argues, is difficult to explain if there is no distinction between Israel and the church.

Godly Advocates

It is worth noting the company of the dispensational position. C. I. Scofield's original intention in his Reference Bible was to help ordinary Christians understand Scripture's prophetic structure. J. Vernon McGee preached through the whole Bible with a warmth and pastoral wisdom that has blessed millions. John MacArthur has defended the pre-tribulation rapture and the literal millennium with careful exegesis and a deep love for the church. These are not fringe figures; they are serious students of Scripture whose convictions deserve a charitable hearing even when we disagree with specific conclusions.
3.examples:
Then: John Nelson Darby developed his system in the 1830s from wrestling seriously with Scripture — particularly with what he saw as the failure of the church to keep distinct the promises made to Israel and those made to the church. He was not, as critics sometimes suggest, simply inventing novelties; he was responding to a real exegetical problem: what do we do with the vast body of Old Testament prophetic promise that seems to remain unfulfilled? His answer — that these promises await a future fulfilment for national Israel in the millennium — is a serious theological response, not a caprice. The Scofield Reference Bible (1909) made these ideas accessible to millions, and the Dallas Theological Seminary tradition (Chafer, Walvoord, Ryrie, Pentecost) developed them into a rigorous theological system that has been deeply influential in evangelical seminaries, mission agencies, and churches.

Now: It is worth acknowledging that significant revision has taken place within dispensationalism itself. "Progressive dispensationalism" (Craig Blaising, Darrell Bock, Robert Saucy) has moved substantially toward recognising that the kingdom is inaugurated in Christ's present reign, that the church is more continuous with Israel than classical dispensationalism allowed, and that the Israel-church distinction, while real, is less absolute than earlier formulations maintained. This internal reform suggests that dispensational scholars are genuinely wrestling with the biblical text and not simply defending a system. Christians of different eschatological convictions can learn from one another — and dispensationalism's passion for the fulfilment of God's promises to Israel, its expectation of Christ's imminent return, and its missionary urgency are gifts to the whole church.

verseByVerse.ref: The Rapture — Caught Up to Meet the Lord
verseByVerse.quote: Then we who are alive, who are left, will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air, and so we will always be with the Lord. — 1 Thessalonians 4:17
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the passage on which the doctrine of the rapture is built, and it deserves to be read carefully and sympathetically. Paul describes something astonishing: believers caught up into the clouds to meet the Lord in the air — a sudden, supernatural event in which the dead in Christ are raised and the living are transformed. The Greek word harpazō — "caught up," from which the Latin rapturo and our word "rapture" derives — is a word of sudden, powerful seizure. This is not a gradual process; it is an instantaneous divine act.

The dispensationalist notes that Paul here describes believers meeting the Lord "in the air" — not on the earth — and that the passage does not describe Christ completing His descent to earth. He meets His people in the air and takes them to be with Him. This, combined with Jesus's promise "I will come again and will take you to myself, that where I am you may be also" (John 14:3), suggests a removal of the church prior to the events of the tribulation. The promise of 1 Thessalonians 5:9 — "God has not destined us for wrath" — reinforces the conviction that the church will be kept from the coming period of God's wrath. Whatever one concludes about the pre-tribulation timing, the event itself — the bodily catching up of the saints to be with the Lord — is the shared hope of all evangelical eschatologies, and Paul's purpose in describing it is identical in all readings: "encourage one another with these words" (v.18).

verseByVerse.ref: God Has Not Rejected His People Israel
verseByVerse.quote: I ask, then, has God rejected his people? By no means! For I myself am an Israelite, a descendant of Abraham, a member of the tribe of Benjamin. God has not rejected his people whom he foreknew. — Romans 11:1–2
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul's passionate denial — "by no means!" — is among the strongest in all his letters. He has just described Israel's stumbling and the Gentiles' reception of the gospel, and the question arises: has God abandoned Israel? His answer is categorical: no. And the ground is the word "foreknew" — a covenantal, electing love that is irreversible. The people God foreknew are not a people He will abandon. This is the bedrock of the dispensationalist's insistence on a future for national Israel: God's covenant with Israel is unconditional and eternal; His purposes for the Jewish people are not exhausted by the present remnant that has come to faith.

The chapter goes on to describe Israel's rejection as temporary (v.12: "their trespass means riches for the world"), reversible (v.23: "if they do not continue in their unbelief, they will be grafted in"), and purposeful for the Gentiles (v.11: "through their trespass salvation has come to the Gentiles"). Paul speaks of Israel's "full inclusion" (v.12) and of being "grafted back into their own olive tree" (v.24) in terms that seem to anticipate something larger than just the ongoing salvation of individual Jewish people. The dispensationalist reads this as pointing to a future national turning of Israel to Christ — and does not see this as incompatible with the gospel but as its ultimate triumph among the covenant people through whom it came.

verseByVerse.ref: The Promises to Israel — Literal Land and Kingdom
verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD came to Abram in a vision: 'Fear not, Abram, I am your shield; your reward shall be very great.' ... On that day the LORD made a covenant with Abram, saying, 'To your offspring I give this land, from the river of Egypt to the great river, the river Euphrates...' — Genesis 15:1, 18
verseByVerse.commentary:
The covenant God made with Abraham in Genesis 15 — ratified by the extraordinary ceremony of the smoking pot and flaming torch passing between the cut animals — included specific, concrete promises: a land with defined borders, descendants as numerous as the stars, and blessing for the world through his seed. The land promise — from Egypt to the Euphrates — was geographical and specific. The dispensationalist asks: was this promise fulfilled? Partially, perhaps, under Solomon — but never in its fullest extent and never permanently. If God's promises are literal when they deal with things already accomplished (Abraham did have a son; his descendants did go to Egypt and be delivered; they did receive Canaan), consistency demands that unfulfilled elements of the promise await a literal future fulfilment.

This is the pastoral heart of the dispensational argument: the faithfulness of God is at stake. If God promised Abraham a land and a kingdom that have never been fully and permanently given, then the promise must be outstanding — awaiting the millennium, when Christ will reign from Jerusalem and Israel will be restored. The alternative — spiritualising the land promise so that it becomes "the whole earth" or "the new creation" — feels to the dispensationalist like robbing Abraham of what God specifically promised him. Whatever one concludes, the question being asked is serious and the concern for divine faithfulness is genuine.

verseByVerse.ref: Saved, So as Through Fire — Not Destined for Wrath
verseByVerse.quote: For God has not destined us for wrath, but to obtain salvation through our Lord Jesus Christ, who died for us so that whether we are awake or asleep we might live with him. — 1 Thessalonians 5:9–10
verseByVerse.commentary:
The pre-tribulation rapture is not merely a system-driven deduction; it is felt by those who hold it as a profound pastoral comfort grounded in the character of God. The God who "has not destined us for wrath" is the God who removed Noah before the flood, rescued Lot before Sodom's destruction, and kept the Israelites safe while the plagues fell on Egypt. The pattern of Scripture, the dispensationalist argues, is that God removes His people from the sphere of His judicial wrath before it falls.

The tribulation period, understood as a time of unprecedented divine judgment on a Christ-rejecting world (Rev 6–19), is precisely such a sphere of wrath. The promise that the church is "not destined for wrath" therefore implies removal from that period. Revelation 3:10's promise to keep the faithful "from the hour of trial" reinforces this: the hour is the tribulation, and keeping "from" it means not enduring it but being exempted from it. The pastoral comfort this offers is real and should be honoured even by those who hold different positions: the confidence that the people of God are in the hands of a God who does not pour His wrath on His own children is a comfort that transcends eschatological systems. The specific question of pre-tribulation timing can be held with appropriate humility while the underlying conviction — God protects His own — is held with great confidence.

4.title: Postmillennialism
4.overview:
Postmillennialism holds that Christ will return after (post-) a millennium — a long period of gospel advance and kingdom expansion in which the gospel progressively transforms the world, the nations are discipled, and the conditions of the earth come to approximate the blessings of the kingdom. The millennium is not a fixed thousand years but an extended era of Christian civilisation and gospel triumph, at the end of which Christ returns to conduct the final judgment and inaugurate the eternal state.

This is an optimistic eschatology — some would say the most optimistic: it believes that the gospel will eventually and substantially win, that nations will be discipled, that evil will be restrained and righteousness advanced, and that Christ's reign will be visibly and progressively acknowledged in the world before His return. The Great Commission will be substantially accomplished; the kingdoms of this world will become the kingdom of our Lord (Rev 11:15) in a real historical sense before the end.

Postmillennialism has a distinguished Reformed pedigree: Jonathan Edwards held a form of it, as did Charles Hodge, B. B. Warfield, and Loraine Boettner. It was influential in the great missionary movements of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries (William Carey's expectation of world evangelisation). It experienced a revival in the late twentieth century through R. J. Rushdoony's reconstructionism and, more moderately, through Keith Mathison's Postmillennialism: An Eschatology of Hope and Douglas Wilson. It tends to produce a strongly world-transforming, culture-engaging Christianity.
4.theology:
The Millennium as Gospel Age

Postmillennialism understands the millennium as the present age of the gospel extended to its full scope — the period during which the gospel reaches all nations and transforms them. Unlike amillennialism, postmillennialism expects a qualitative improvement in the state of the world before Christ's return: a golden age of Christian faith, justice, and culture, not merely a continuation of the mixed present pattern of advance and resistance. The thousand years of Revelation 20 may refer to this golden age specifically, or it may be a symbolic number for the whole gospel age.

The Great Commission and the Psalms

Postmillennialists find their strongest positive evidence not in Revelation but in the Psalms (especially Psalm 2, 22, 72, 110) and in the Great Commission (Matt 28:18–20). Psalm 110:1 — "The LORD says to my Lord: 'Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool'" — is understood as describing a present, progressive conquest: Christ is currently reigning and His enemies are being progressively subdued through the advance of the gospel. The Great Commission's promise that "all authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me" (Matt 28:18) grounds the expectation that the commission will be substantially accomplished: the one with all authority has commanded it, and all authority guarantees its success.

The Mustard Seed Parables

The parables of Matthew 13 — the mustard seed that grows into a great tree (v.31–32), the leaven that leavens the whole lump (v.33) — are read by postmillennialists as descriptions of the kingdom's eventual comprehensive triumph in history: from small and seemingly insignificant beginnings, the kingdom will fill the whole earth. The amillennialist reads these as describing the kingdom's universal reach (it will spread to all nations) without necessarily implying comprehensive cultural transformation.
4.examples:
Then: Jonathan Edwards developed a robust postmillennialism rooted in the Psalms and the promises of Isaiah. He expected the millennium to be a future golden age of gospel expansion, beginning perhaps in America, from which the gospel would transform the world. His "History of the Work of Redemption" is the most sustained American theological vision of world history as the progressive triumph of the gospel. B. B. Warfield, the great Princeton theologian, held a moderate postmillennialism, insisting that the gospel's power, applied by the Spirit, was equal to the task of transforming the world. William Carey's missionary vision — "Expect great things from God; attempt great things for God" — was fuelled by postmillennial confidence that the gospel would prevail globally.

Now: Two world wars, the Holocaust, the persistence of global suffering, and the decline of Christianity in the West have made postmillennialism less credible to many. The confident optimism of nineteenth-century missionary postmillennialism seems hard to sustain in the face of history. Postmillennialists respond that the historical scope of the gospel advance is not measured in decades but in centuries, and that the perspective of two thousand years of church history — with the gospel now present in every nation on earth — is more encouraging than a focus on any particular century's setbacks. The question is one of historical horizon and of how one weighs Scripture's promises against present experience.

verseByVerse.quote: May all kings fall down before him, all nations serve him!... May his name endure forever, his fame continue as long as the sun! May people be blessed in him, all nations call him blessed! — Psalm 72:11, 17
verseByVerse.commentary:
Psalm 72 is a royal psalm, written for or about Solomon but pointing beyond him to the ultimate Davidic King — the Messiah. The scope of the psalm is breathtaking: all kings, all nations, all the earth blessing and serving Him. The postmillennialist takes this as a promise of historical, terrestrial, pre-parousia fulfilment: the gospel will advance until all nations are genuinely discipled, all kings acknowledge the Lord, and the blessing of Abraham (Gen 12:3) reaches every corner of the earth within history. This is not a description of the eternal state but of the messianic age — the millennium of gospel triumph.

The amillennialist does not dispute the promise; they dispute its mode of fulfilment. All nations will indeed be blessed in Him — through the preaching of the gospel, the gathering of a people from every tribe and tongue (Rev 7:9), and the consummation in the new creation. The difference is whether the comprehensive blessing happens before Christ's return (postmillennial) or at and after it (amillennial). The Psalm itself does not specify the timing; it proclaims the certainty of the King's universal dominion — and on that both agree.

verseByVerse.quote: He put another parable before them, saying, 'The kingdom of heaven is like a grain of mustard seed that a man took and sowed in his field. It is the smallest of all seeds, but when it has grown it is larger than all the garden plants and becomes a tree, so that the birds of the air come and make nests in its branches.' — Matthew 13:31–32
verseByVerse.commentary:
The postmillennialist reads the mustard seed parable as a promise of the kingdom's eventual comprehensive dominion within history. From the smallest of beginnings — a wandering teacher in first-century Palestine, twelve disciples, a handful of persecuted early churches — the kingdom will grow into something that encompasses and shelters the whole world. "The birds of the air come and make nests in its branches" echoes Daniel 4:12 and Ezekiel 17:23 — language used of universal empire. The kingdom will be, in historical terms, the great tree that fills the earth.

The amillennial and historic premillennial readings see the same growth but interpret "becomes a tree" as reaching its full scope (all nations) rather than its full dominion (all cultural realms). The parable is about the unexpected greatness that will come from small beginnings — which all positions affirm. The postmillennial reading pushes further: not merely worldwide in reach but transformatively dominant in cultural and social influence. The leaven parable (v.33) reinforces this: as leaven works through the whole lump invisibly and comprehensively, so the gospel will permeate and transform the entire fabric of human society.

verseByVerse.ref: The Earth Shall Be Full of the Knowledge of the LORD
verseByVerse.quote: They shall not hurt or destroy in all my holy mountain; for the earth shall be full of the knowledge of the LORD as the waters cover the sea. — Isaiah 11:9
verseByVerse.commentary:
Isaiah 11 is a messianic prophecy describing the reign of the shoot from the stump of Jesse (v.1) — the Messiah who judges with righteousness, who destroys the wicked, and under whose reign the wolf lies down with the lamb (v.6) and a little child leads them (v.6). Verse 9 is the postmillennialist's great promise: the earth full of the knowledge of the Lord — not a partial reach, not a remnant, but comprehensive, total, covering the earth as waters cover the sea.

Does this describe a pre-parousia golden age (postmillennialism), the eternal state (amillennialism), or the millennial reign of Christ after His return (premillennialism)? The postmillennialist argues from the earthly, historical character of the imagery: this is not the eternal state but the earth, with its nations and kings, transformed by the presence of the Messiah's knowledge. Isaiah 11 is a promise for history, not merely for eternity. The other positions note that "the earth" in Isaiah's eschatological vision often includes what we would call the new creation — a renewed cosmos that is simultaneously the fulfilment of the present earth and something gloriously beyond it.

verseByVerse.quote: The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, and he shall reign forever and ever. — Revelation 11:15
verseByVerse.commentary:
The seventh trumpet announces what is presented in Revelation as a done deal: the kingdom of the world has become (aorist tense — a completed act) the kingdom of the Lord and of His Christ. The postmillennialist reads this as the culmination of the gospel's historical conquest — the moment when the comprehensive advance of the kingdom reaches its completion, and Christ's reign over all the earth is acknowledged. The missionary mandate is the mechanism; the seventh trumpet is the announcement of its completion.

Most interpreters, however, place the seventh trumpet at or near the end of history — whether at Christ's return (amillennial/premillennial) or at the transition to the eternal state. The postmillennialist reads it as the climax of historical gospel advance that precedes the return; others read it as the return itself, or the announcement of what the return accomplishes. What all positions affirm is the certainty of the outcome: the kingdoms of this world will become the kingdom of our Lord. The gospel will not fail; Christ's reign will not be thwarted; the earth and its peoples will ultimately submit to the King — whether in willing worship or unwilling judgment. That certainty is the ground of the church's confidence in mission, whatever one's millennial view.

5.title: A Reformed Assessment
5.overview:
Having presented all four eschatological models as fairly as possible, it is time to ask how to navigate the genuine disagreements — with charity toward those who differ, clarity about the questions that matter most, and confidence in what Scripture speaks most plainly. This unit offers a Reformed assessment — not an ecclesiastical verdict that condemns those who disagree, but the considered judgment of a tradition with deep biblical and theological roots, offered in a spirit of service to the whole church.

Christians across all four positions love the same Lord, submit to the same Scripture, and look forward to the same blessed hope: the personal, visible, glorious return of Jesus Christ. That shared conviction is more important than any millennial disagreement. A congregation that contains amillennialists, historic premillennialists, postmillennialists, and dispensationalists is a congregation united by the things that matter most — the gospel, the lordship of Christ, and the expectation of His return — and divided only at the level of secondary interpretation of difficult prophetic texts. That is not a cause for division; it is a cause for humble, mutually enriching conversation.

What follows reflects the mainstream Reformed tradition's conclusions, offered not to silence other voices but to provide a framework for thinking through the questions with care. The tradition has learned from the debate, and continues to learn. Even those who ultimately find the amillennial reading most persuasive have been sharpened by dispensationalism's insistence on the specificity of God's promises and its passion for the literal fulfilment of Scripture.
5.theology:
What All Four Positions Share

Before noting differences, the common ground deserves to be stated clearly and emphatically. All four positions affirm: (1) The visible, bodily, glorious return of Jesus Christ — personal, public, and unmistakable. (2) The bodily resurrection of the dead — righteous and wicked — to face final judgment. (3) The final judgment of all people — each accountable before the King. (4) The eternal state — new creation for the redeemed, eternal separation for the unrepentant. (5) The complete trustworthiness of every promise God has made. (6) The urgency of the gospel mission before the end. These are not peripheral matters; they are the load-bearing structure of Christian eschatology, and all four positions build on them.

Where the Reformed Tradition Comes Down

Within this shared framework, the Reformed tradition has historically favoured amillennialism — reading Revelation 20 as describing the present gospel age, understanding the new covenant church as the fulfilment of the promises made to Israel in Christ, and expecting one general resurrection and judgment at Christ's return. It has also welcomed historic premillennialism and postmillennialism as live options within the Reformed family. Where the tradition has been most consistently cautious is about the dispensational separation of Israel and the church as two distinct peoples with two distinct eternal destinies — not because the concern for Israel is wrong (it is right and biblical) but because the New Testament seems to present the church as the one new humanity in Christ, incorporating believing Jews and Gentiles into a single covenant people (Eph 2:11–22).

The Hermeneutical Question

The deepest disagreement is hermeneutical: how should Old Testament prophecy be read? The dispensational instinct — read it as literally as possible — flows from a genuine reverence for Scripture and a genuine concern for God's faithfulness to His promises. The covenant-theological instinct — read Old Testament prophecy through the lens of its New Testament fulfilment — flows from a conviction that the apostles themselves model this approach, regularly applying Old Testament texts to Christ and the church in ways that transcend wooden literalism. Neither approach is cavalier; both deserve serious engagement.
5.examples:
Lessons the Tradition Has Learned from Dispensationalism

It would be ungenerous and unwise to engage dispensationalism only critically. The tradition has genuine debts to pay. Dispensationalism's passion for detailed engagement with Old Testament prophecy has kept the church from a lazy spiritualising that treats the Hebrew Scriptures as merely a source of moral illustrations. Its insistence on the specificity of God's promises has challenged covenant theologians to give a more careful account of what "fulfilment" means and how Christ fulfils without abrogating the Old Testament. Its concern for the Jewish people has been a persistent and valuable corrective to the anti-Semitism that has periodically stained the church's history. And its expectation of an imminent return has fuelled a missionary urgency — "the Lord could come at any moment" — that has sent thousands to the field.

Holding the Debate with Grace

A pastor serving a congregation with diverse eschatological convictions will do well to: (1) Preach clearly on the certainties — return, resurrection, judgment, new creation — with confidence and pastoral warmth. (2) Handle the disputed questions with intellectual honesty, presenting the best arguments on each side rather than caricaturing those who differ. (3) Model genuine curiosity and humility — the millennial question has occupied the greatest biblical scholars of every age without reaching consensus, which should produce in us appropriate modesty. (4) Unite the congregation around the prayer that transcends all eschatological systems: maranatha — Come, Lord Jesus. Whatever the shape of the path from here to there, the destination and the One we are waiting for are the same.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, he is coming with the clouds, and every eye will see him, even those who pierced him, and all tribes of the earth will wail on account of him. Even so. Amen. — Revelation 1:7
verseByVerse.commentary:
This verse is the one eschatological certainty that all four millennial positions affirm without reservation, and it deserves to anchor every conversation about the end times. The return of Christ will be visible, universal, and public — not a secret departure, not a quiet spiritual presence, but a coming with clouds that every eye will see. The language combines Daniel 7:13 (the Son of Man coming with the clouds of heaven) and Zechariah 12:10 (they will look on the one they have pierced) — the glorified King and the crucified Servant, arriving in the same moment.

The "wailing" of verse 7 is the response of those confronted with the One they rejected — whether in the first century or at the end of history, all those who did not receive Him will see Him and know, finally and irrevocably, who He is. John's "even so, amen" is not passive acceptance but active longing — the church's prayer from the beginning: it is good and right that the King should come, that the books should be opened, that the wrong should be righted, that the rejected One should be universally acknowledged. Whatever one's millennial position, this is the hope. Come, Lord Jesus.

verseByVerse.ref: Israel and the Fullness of the Gentiles
verseByVerse.quote: Lest you be wise in your own sight, I do not want you to be unaware of this mystery, brothers: a partial hardening has come upon Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles has come in. And in this way all Israel will be saved... — Romans 11:25–26
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the passage where the eschatological traditions most sharply divide — and where the dispensationalist makes some of the strongest points. Paul calls this a "mystery" — something not fully disclosed in the Old Testament, now revealed: Israel's hardening is partial and temporary, conditioned on the fullness of Gentile inclusion. "All Israel will be saved" follows this fullness — and whatever exactly Paul means, he clearly means more than merely the present remnant. The dispensationalist argues that this describes a future national turning of Israel to Christ, connected to His return.

The covenant-theological tradition has generally read "all Israel" as the full number of the elect — both Jews and Gentiles who make up the true Israel of God (Gal 6:16) — or as a future large-scale conversion of Jewish people that is not a separate national programme but a remarkable work of the Spirit within the one Covenant of Grace. What all traditions should share is Paul's own pastoral conclusion: marvel at the mystery (v.33), do not be arrogant toward Jewish people (v.18–20), and pray for their salvation (10:1). The doctrine of Romans 11 is not primarily a chart to be plotted but a call to humility, wonder, and intercession for the people through whom the Messiah came.

verseByVerse.ref: The Day of the Lord — Suddenly and Certainly
verseByVerse.quote: But the day of the Lord will come like a thief, and then the heavens will pass away with a roar, and the heavenly bodies will be burned up and dissolved, and the earth and the works that are done on it will be exposed. — 2 Peter 3:10
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter's description of the day of the Lord has two pastoral emphases that all eschatological traditions affirm: its certainty and its suddenness. Scoffers in Peter's day were saying, "Where is the promise of his coming?" (v.4) — mocking the expectation of a return that had not happened. Peter's answer is not a revised timeline but a theological response: God's patience is not delay; it is mercy, giving space for repentance (v.9). When the day comes, it will come suddenly — like a thief — and it will be comprehensive in its judgment.

The practical question Peter draws from this is the same whatever one's millennial position: "What sort of people ought you to be?" (v.11). Holy and godly lives. Waiting and hastening the coming day. Diligent to be found at peace, without spot or blemish (v.14). The eschatological ethics of the New Testament consistently focus not on speculative chronology but on present faithfulness. Whether one expects a rapture before the tribulation, endurance through the tribulation, or a gradual gospel triumph before the return, the call of 2 Peter 3 is the same: live in light of the coming King, hold this world loosely, and pursue the holiness that will be consummated when He comes.

verseByVerse.quote: Our Lord, come! — 1 Corinthians 16:22 / 'Come, Lord Jesus!' — Revelation 22:20
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Aramaic prayer maranatha — "our Lord, come!" — is one of the oldest Christian prayers, preserved by Paul in its original Aramaic because it was already the universal prayer of the first Christian communities. It closes the New Testament in its Greek form: "Come, Lord Jesus" (Rev 22:20). It is the eschatological prayer of the church in every age — and it is the prayer that every genuine Christian, whatever their millennial position, is praying. It acknowledges that the King has not yet returned, that history is not yet complete, and that His return is the deepest longing of those who love Him.

This prayer is the best place to end any conversation about eschatology — not because it resolves the debates but because it reorients them. The dispensationalist who prays "Come, Lord Jesus" and the amillennialist who prays "Come, Lord Jesus" and the postmillennialist who prays "Come, Lord Jesus" are all praying to the same Lord, awaiting the same return, longing for the same consummation. The shape of the path from here to that moment is what they disagree about. But the destination — and the One they are waiting for — is the same. And on the day He comes, every difference of interpretation will be resolved, every longing will be fulfilled, and every eye will see what every heart has hoped for. Even so, come, Lord Jesus. Amen.
